nameStory: The Amber-winged Spreadwing gets its name from the beautiful golden-amber tint that often colors its wings, especially noticeable when sunlight shines through them. The 'spreadwing' part refers to how this damselfly holds its wings at a distinctive angle away from its body when resting, rather than folding them neatly alongside like most other damselflies do.
description: The Amber-winged Spreadwing is a slender damselfly with delicate wings that often show a warm, amber-colored tinge. Like all damselflies, it has a thin body and four wings of roughly equal size, but what makes spreadwings special is how they rest with their wings held at about a 45-degree angle from their body. Adults are typically around 1.5 to 2 inches long with a wingspan of about 2 inches. These graceful insects are predators that catch smaller flying insects on the wing.

idTips.label: Wing Position
idTips.description: When resting, wings are held at about a 45-degree angle from the body, creating a distinctive 'V' shape when viewed from above - very different from most damselflies that fold wings alongside their body

idTips.label: Wing Color
idTips.description: Wings often have a noticeable amber or golden tint, especially visible when backlit by sunlight - hold up your hand behind the insect to see this effect clearly

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Slender, needle-like body that feels delicate if gently handled - much thinner than a dragonfly and about as thick as a pencil lead

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Weak, fluttering flight that looks almost hesitant compared to the strong, direct flight of dragonflies - often hovers near vegetation

idTips.label: Eye Position
idTips.description: Large eyes positioned on the sides of the head rather than touching in the middle, giving a more delicate appearance than dragonflies

habitat: Look for Amber-winged Spreadwings around ponds, slow streams, marshes, and other quiet freshwater areas with plenty of emergent vegetation like cattails and sedges. They prefer areas with some tree cover nearby and are often found in woodland ponds or wetlands surrounded by forest. The adults spend much of their time perching on vegetation near the water's edge.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, usually in May, as water temperatures warm. Fresh adults may appear pale and less distinctly colored at first.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in summer when adults are most abundant and actively mating. This is the best time to observe their distinctive wing-spreading behavior and amber coloration.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, though numbers decline. Late-season individuals may appear more worn with tattered wing edges.
seasonality.winter: No adults present - the species overwinters as eggs laid in plant stems near water, waiting for spring warmth to hatch.

funFact: The name 'Lestes' comes from the ancient Greek word for 'thief' - but these damselflies aren't stealing anything from us, they're actually beneficial predators that help control mosquito and midge populations around wetlands!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other spreadwing species, but the amber wing tint is a good clue when present. Remember: if the wings are held alongside the body when resting, it's not a spreadwing at all - those are broad-winged or pond damselflies from different families.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that damselflies and dragonflies are actually quite different - damselflies are generally smaller, more delicate, and fold or angle their wings when resting, while dragonflies are bulkier and always hold their wings straight out horizontally.
compareHints: Among New England's spreadwings, the Amber-winged is distinguished by its wing coloration when present, though this can be subtle. The Emerald Spreadwing has a more metallic green sheen to its body, while the Slender Spreadwing is typically smaller and more delicate-looking. Size, habitat preferences, and subtle body coloration differences help separate the various Lestes species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's spreadwings, the Slender Spreadwing is distinguished by its exceptionally thin body profile and pale blue face coloration.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Spotted Spreadwing is one of the easier ones to identify thanks to its distinctive wing spots.
Among New England's nine Lestes species, Swamp Spreadwings are distinguished by their strong preference for heavily vegetated wetlands and their larger, more robust build.
Among New England's spreadwings, the elegant spreadwing is distinguished by its bronze-brown coloration and medium size.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Northern Spreadwing is distinguished by its preference for more permanent water bodies compared to species like the Swamp Spreadwing which favors temporary pools.
Among New England's spreadwings, the Emerald Spreadwing stands out for its brilliant metallic green coloration - most others like the Swamp Spreadwing appear more bronze or brown.
Among New England spreadwings, sweetflag spreadwings are distinguished by their preference for heavily vegetated wetlands rather than open water.
